comments.author: freeCodeCamp
comments.comment:
Most agent failures I see are not model failures, they are state failures. The harness needs typed tool contracts, replayable traces, and a budget for context compaction, because one lossy summary can quietly corrupt the next tool call. What checks do you run before letting an agent write to a real system?

#AgenticAI

comments.author: Sairam Sundaresan
comments.comment: The quiet failure I see most: eval sets freeze while the corpus keeps changing. For RAG, I like tracking retrieval misses separately from answer faithfulness, because a perfect generator cannot recover evidence the retriever never surfaced. What threshold do you use before blocking a release?

comments.author: Sitaraman Subramanian
comments.comment: The real shift is not longer context or better prompting, it is moving from “model returns text” to “system owns a loop”: plan, call tools, inspect state, recover, and stop. The hard part is usually not the agent logic, it is sandbox boundaries, evals for tool side effects, and replayable traces when something fails. What do you think becomes the default control plane here: model provider native, or a thin app-owned orchestration layer on top?

comments.author: Maryam Bahrami
comments.comment: `/diff` is the one I’d keep if I had to pick only one. The failure mode in agentic coding is rarely “no code was written”, it’s “the change looks plausible but quietly moved a boundary.” Diff review keeps the human in the loop at the exact point where judgment matters.
